MOBILE AUDIO DIAGNOSTIC

Test procedure

  1. Turn the phone's media volume up.
  2. Leave the Ring/Silent setting where it is now for the first pass.
  3. Press tests 1 to 5, one at a time, and listen after each.
  4. After every test press HEARD IT or DID NOT HEAR IT.
  5. Press COPY RESULTS and send them back.
  6. If this phone has a Ring/Silent switch or a silent/vibrate mode, reload the page and repeat the whole run with that setting flipped. Not every phone has one.

Nothing plays until you press a button. Every test plays the same 660 Hz beep, about 0.4 seconds.

FOR TEST 6: TURN IPHONE SILENT MODE ON.
Keep the media volume turned up. Test 6 checks whether Web Audio becomes audible despite Silent mode once the audio session is set to "playback".

TESTS 7 AND 8 ARE THE IMPORTANT ONES NOW.
They reproduce the real game: the actual background music looping through a DOM <audio> element while Web Audio catch sounds fire over it. Run 7 first, then 8, and answer both.

Device / runtime

1. Web Audio — play now

Oscillator created and started synchronously inside the tap. No timer, no promise, no animation frame before start(). Tests whether Web Audio can make sound at all on this device.

NOT TESTED
-

2. Web Audio — play after 2 seconds

Context resumed from the real tap, but the oscillator starts 2 seconds later, outside the gesture. Compares trusted-gesture Web Audio with later programmatic use.

NOT TESTED
-

3. DOM <audio> — play now

One real <audio playsinline preload="auto"> element that is in the page markup. play() is called directly in the tap. No pool.

NOT TESTED
-

4. Same DOM <audio> — replay after 2 seconds

The exact same element as test 3. Plays once from the tap (result A), then 2 seconds later rewinds and plays again programmatically (result B). This is the pattern the game uses for a catch sound, and it is the critical test.

NOT TESTED
-

5. Detached new Audio() — play now

One new Audio(...) that is never added to the page. play() called directly in the tap. Isolates DOM element vs detached element.

NOT TESTED
-

6. Web Audio + audioSession “playback”

Run this one with iPhone Silent mode ON. Sets navigator.audioSession.type = "playback" synchronously in the tap, then plays the same beep as test 1 — once immediately, and once 2 seconds later. This determines whether the original Web Audio catch sounds can be heard while Silent mode is on.

7. GAME CONDITIONS — the game’s own tones over the real music

The closest reproduction of the actual game. In the tap it does exactly what the game does, in the same order: sets navigator.audioSession.type = "playback", creates the AudioContext, primes it with a 1-sample silent buffer, then starts the real background music track looping through a DOM <audio> element at the game’s own volume 0.22. Then, 3 seconds later with the music already playing, it fires the game’s exact catch tones: the Water pickup (triangle 505→858.5 Hz, gain 0.17, 0.16 s), then the Bomb (sawtooth 180→38 Hz, gain 0.22, 0.50 s).

NOT TESTED

B — the BOMB tone (low growl):

8. Same conditions — but the LOUD tone

Identical setup to test 7 — same AudioContext, same looping music at 0.22 — but it plays the loud sustained 660 Hz tone from tests 1–6 (gain 0.35, held for 0.34 s) instead of the game’s tones. Run test 7 first, then this one.

What the pair proves: 7 silent + 8 audible → the game’s tones are too quiet/short to hear over the music. Both silent → the AudioContext itself is dead under game conditions. Both audible → this page does not reproduce the failure, and the next step is instrumenting the real game.
